thread.title: Intraday Update: Everything Is Awesome…and the Dow Doesn’t Care - Barron's

author: Brett Arends
title: Intraday Update: Everything Is Awesome…and the Dow Doesn’t Care - Barron's
text:
By Brett Arends Updated April 27, 2018 1:27 p.m. ET Do you want to hear something ominous? Everything is positive - and Wall Street doesn’t care.
Illustration: Getty Images The first quarter gross domestic product figures came positive. Corporations are crushing earnings . Consumer confidence is up. Wages are accelerating. Peace appears at long last to have broken out on the Korean peninsula . And the ten-year Treasury yield is tumbling again, well back below the 3% threshold , which should be good for mortgage lending, home prices, and corporate borrowing.
And stocks?
By lunchtime the morning’s initial gains had evaporated. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down around 30 points around midday, after falling just over 100 points in mid-morning. The Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 were both barely in positive territory.
So-called market internals make for even less cheerful reading. Falling stocks outnumbered rising ones across the NYSE and NASDAQ during the morning, by 2797 to 2657. Breadth at least was positive, with volumes on rising stocks slightly exceeding that on falling ones.
Yes, it’s depressing. As Bespoke Investment Group observes, wages and salaries are now rising at their fastest annual rate since the start of the economic expansion, and the figures are good even when you strip out volatile incentive-paid occupations. Yet markets are flat.
Is all the good news already reflected in high stock prices?
Clouds appear to be gathering over Cupertino: Apple (AAPL), the most popular and valuable stock on the planet, fell another 1.5% ahead of Tuesday’s earnings amid growing fears that the flagship $1,000 iPhone X is selling well below hopes . Amazon (AMZN) is up 5% after trouncing earnings overnight . Other popular big tech companies were in the red. Twitter (TWTR) fell 5%, Snap 3%, and Alphabet (GOOG) and Netflix (NFLX) were off about 1%. Tesla (TSLA), on the other hand, gained 1%.
Economist Marc Handler notes that the U.S. Dollar is finishing its best week in five months, and has now risen for 10 of the past thirteen weeks. There are two things really bullish about the greenback. The first is so many people were bearish that there was plenty of room for reaction. The second is that Larry “King Dollar” Kudlow, who passionately believes in a high dollar, recently took over as chief economic adviser to the president. Trump can be easily persuaded, no doubt, that a strong or “winning” dollar is somehow a reflection of national pride rather than a problem for U.S. exports .
S&P 500 : +0.2% to 2673.44
Dow 30 : +13.09, or 0.1%, to 24,335.43
Nasdaq : +0.1% to 7127.35
Vix : -2.9% to 15.77
10-year Treasury Yield : -0.03 percentage point to 2.96%
Midday Movers Charter Communications (CHTR) is down 15.3%, to $252.69 after dropping to a new 52-week low, the worst performer in the S&P 500 at recent check, after reporting first-quarter earnings . It earned 70 cents a share on revenue of $10.66 billion, while analysts were looking for earnings of 46 cents a share on revenue of $10.62 billion. However, weak subscriber metrics sank the stock.
Discover Financial Services (DFS) is down 1.2% to $71.50 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The credit card firm earned $1.82 a share on revenue of $2.58 billion, while analysts were looking for earnings of $1.77 a share on revenue of $2.58 billion.
Mattel (MAT) is up 6.9% to $14.95 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The toy maker lost 60 cents a share on revenue of $708.4 million. Analysts were expecting a 39 cent per-share loss, one revenue of $687.7 million.
Regenron Pharmaceuticals (REGN) is down 6.5% to $303.07 after partner Sanofi (SNY), down 2.8% to $39.25, reported first-quarter earnings : Drugs Dupixent, Praluent, and Kevzara all missed estimates.
SVB Financial (SIVB) is up 17.3% to $301.80, after notching a new 52-week high, making it the best performer in the S&P 500 at recent check, following its first-quarter earnings. The financial firm earned $3.63 a share, well above the $3.15 per-share consensus estimate. — Teresa Rivas
